metadata.title: School effectiveness and high reading achievement of Spanish students in PISA 2018: a machine learning approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (students aged 15–16) and applies a two-stage analytic strategy: Random Forest classification followed by multilevel binary logistic regression with a student (level 1) and school (level 2) hierarchy. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights, so it is unclear whether complex survey design adjustments were applied in either stage. For the Random Forest stage, the authors describe multiple imputation, standardisation, and cross-validation, but do not mention weight-aware estimation; many ML implementations are run without survey weights unless explicitly supported. For the multilevel logistic regression stage, the authors omit schools with 20 or fewer students and report robust standard errors, but they still do not specify any PISA weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) being used; analysts using the OECD database should consider applying the appropriate PISA student weights when estimating population-representative effects.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is restricted to Spanish students participating in PISA 2018 (initially 35,943 students). For the multilevel logistic regression stage, schools with 20 or fewer students were omitted, eliminating 1,532 students across 133 schools and yielding a refined sample of 34,411 students across 976 schools. The dependent variable is dichotomised to identify high performers in reading literacy (PISA levels 5–6) versus average/low (levels below 5). Predictors are drawn from 159 questionnaire/derived indices, then reduced to 137 by removing variables with >20% missingness, except learning-time variables (LMMINS/MMINS/SMINS) which were retained despite ~24–25% missingness. Missing predictor values were imputed prior to model fitting.

confounders_identified.variable_name: ICT as topic in social interaction

top_predictors: Learning time in science (minutes per week)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (validation sample): best candidate set (15 variables) AUC = 0.839; Accuracy = 0.952. Relative importance ranking: enjoyment of reading (100%), metacognition: credibility assessment (86.520%), reading self-concept competence (61.827%), reading self-concept difficulty (39.826%), learning time in science (32.459%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for Spain, the study leveraged enjoyment of reading, metacognition: credibility assessment, reading self-concept (competence and difficulty), and learning time in science to predict high reading performance (levels 5–6), finding that process variables dominated the relative importance ranking (with enjoyment of reading and credibility assessment the top predictors). This indicates that strengthening reading engagement and metacognitive credibility-evaluation skills may be a practical route to increasing the proportion of top-performing readers in Spain, though the results are predictive rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 for Spain, focusing on reading literacy and defining “high performance” as achieving PISA levels 5–6 (vs. average/low). It first fits a Random Forest classifier after multiple imputation by chained equations, standardisation, and 10-fold cross-validation, evaluating models across plausible values and selecting the most accurate PV (PV9 with AUC = 0.827) to report key predictors. In the validation sample, the best candidate set of 15 predictors achieved AUC = 0.839 and Accuracy = 0.952, and the relative-importance ranking shows process variables leading (enjoyment of reading and metacognition: credibility assessment). The subsequent multilevel binary logistic regression (student and school levels) reports explained variance of ~41% for context/input-only, ~38.258% for process-only, and ~54.676% for the combined model, with metacognition: credibility assessment having the largest odds ratio (≈1.989). Limitations include lack of causal interpretation and unclear use of PISA sampling weights.
